title: Per-tenant SLA subsidy worksheet
content:
Purpose: scribble down a simple model for charging/subsidizing per-tenant SLAs. Goal is to produce a lightweight heuristic we can turn into a rule-of-thumb for sales and PMs: how much monthly subsidy (or committed capacity discount) is reasonable for X latency SLO, given workload shape and marginal token cost.

High-level idea: SLA = guarantee of p95 latency under a concurrency envelope + optional reserved capacity. Subsidy can be structured as either a flat monthly credit that offsets usage (credits), or a sustained discount on per-token rates up to a commit. We want a quick conversion between: expected extra infra cost to Redwood for the SLA and suggested customer-facing subsidy.

Assumptions (pick conservative numbers for quick math):
- Baseline cost per million tokens (hosted, post-batching, amortized infra + GPU + networking + ops): $6.5 / 1M tokens (this is approximated from infra + amortized GPU at near-spot pricing).
- Margin target on hosted product: 45% gross. So list-rate cost budget ~ $6.5 / (1 - 0.45) = $11.82 / 1M tokens.
- SLA overhead (when forcing low-latency serving): extra cost comes from lower batching efficiency, reserved GPU slices, warm KV cache. Estimate relative penalty on cost per token: 1) mild SLA (p95 < 250ms): +10% cost, 2) strict SLA (p95 < 100ms): +25%, 3) ultra (p95 < 50ms): +60%. These are knobs we can refine by model family and sequence length.
- SLO sizing: customers buy reserved concurrency units; one unit ~ 100 qps (requests that generate ~200 tokens on average). Use approximate tokens per request = 200 TPQ.
- Typical session distribution: 70% short (<=50 tokens), 25% medium (50-500 tokens), 5% long (>500). SLA penalty mainly driven by short interactions (cannot batch much).

Quick formulas (BOTE):
- baseline_cost_per_token = baseline_millions_cost / 1e6. e.g. $6.5 / 1e6 = $0.0000065 per token.
- adjusted_cost = baseline_cost_per_token * (1 + sla_penalty).
- monthly_tokens = avg_tokens_per_request * requests_per_month.
- monthly_infra_extra = monthly_tokens * baseline_cost_per_token * sla_penalty.
- recommended_subsidy = monthly_infra_extra * subsidy_share (where subsidy_share is the fraction we cover; sales may offer 50-75% of incremental cost depending on strategic value).

Numeric example A — mid-market customer, mild SLA (p95 < 250ms):
- traffic: 500 DAUs, 4 requests/user/day = 2k requests/day = 60k requests/month.
- avg tokens/request = 200 => monthly tokens = 12M tokens.
- baseline infra spend = 12M * $0.0000065 = $78.
- SLA penalty = 10% => extra infra cost = $7.8 / month.
- If we subsidize 70% of extra infra => subsidy ~ $5.5 / month (rounded).
- Observation: tiny numbers at token-level — the main commercial levers are pricing psychology and commitment packaging, not per-customer micro-dollars. But subsidy becomes meaningful at scale.

Numeric example B — startup pilot, strict SLA (p95 < 100ms) for interactive UX:
- traffic: 50k requests/day = 1.5M/month; avg tokens/request = 150 -> monthly tokens = 225M tokens.
- baseline infra spend = 225M * $0.0000065 = $1,462.5.
- SLA penalty = 25% => extra infra cost = $365.6 / month.
- Subsidy at 50% => $182.8 / month credit.
- Alternatively, translate to committed discount: for a 12-month commit of $10k/month, offering a $183/month credit is negligible; instead offer % off tokens or waived setup. So compute subsidy as percent of committed spend is more meaningful for sales.

Per-tenant reserve model (simpler for packaging):
- Offer reserved concurrency slabs (small, medium, large). Each slab corresponds to a soft-guarantee and includes a built-in monthly credit that roughly equals X*expected_extra_cost for that slab.
- Example slabs: Small = 2k rps-month capacity (~1.8M tokens/month), Medium = 10k rps-month (~9M tokens/month), Large = 50k rps-month (~45M tokens/month). Precompute "expected SLA penalty $/month" for each slab per model family. Store these in a table sales can reference.

Heuristic table (BOTE numbers, per month):
- small (mild SLA): tokens 1.8M -> extra infra cost @10% = $1.17 -> subsidy at 60% = $0.70/mo.
- medium (strict SLA): tokens 9M -> extra infra cost @25% = $14.6 -> subsidy @60% = $8.8/mo.
- large (strict SLA): tokens 45M -> extra infra cost @25% = $73 -> subsidy @60% = $44/mo.

Notes on packaging psychology:
- Customers will expect an obvious, round-credit or % discount number. Present subsidy as a round monthly credit or % discount off list rate up to a committed amount.
- For sales, avoid micro-dollar credits (they look weak). Instead: 1) express subsidy as "up to $X off per month" with X rounded to nearest $10 or $50 for small/medium customers; 2) for large customers, show as percent of committed spend (e.g., 1-2% of committed ARR) or as guaranteed concurrency with discounted per-token rates.

Operational levers that change the math:
- Batching improvements (we can shrink the SLA penalty substantially with edge batching or per-tenant micro-queues). If we can reduce penalty for strict SLA from 25% to 12% -> subsidy halves.
- Model quantization/weights: smaller quant models reduce marginal cost by 20-40% depending on accuracy tolerance. Include quantized option in the SLA package.
- Cache priming: warm KV cache for top N prefixes for a tenant reduces their p50/p95 and lowers infra penalty for conversational workloads. This is server cost (state storage) vs compute tradeoff.

Selling constructs to propose:
1) "SLA Credit" — monthly dollar credit that offsets extra infra cost. Simple for pilot customers (<$250/mo). Good for trials.
2) "Reserved Concurrency Slab" — includes guaranteed capacity, a fixed monthly fee, and an included SLA credit (rounded up). Good for mid-market.
3) "Committed ARR + SLA Discount" — multi-month commit where we apply a 1-3% committed-discount that implicitly covers SLA overhead. Good for enterprise.

Quick decision matrix for sales (one-liners):
- If monthly expected extra infra <$50 -> offer SLA Credit (flat, easy).
- If extra infra $50-$5k -> recommend Reserved Slab (round numbers, show included credit, allow burst).
- If extra infra >$5k -> require committed ARR; handle via discount ladder tied to term.

Open questions / experiments to run:
- Empirical measurement of SLA penalty by model family and seq length distribution (run A/B: same traffic under batched vs reserved serving).
- Customer willingness test: run an experiment offering two pilots: (A) $200/mo credit + mild SLO; (B) 10% discount on committed spend + stronger SLO. See which converts.
- Build small calculator in Console: input monthly requests, avg tokens/request, desired p95 -> outputs recommended slab and suggested subsidy (round to nearest $10).

To-do (next steps):
- Ask infra to run a micro-benchmark (toy tenant) for the most common model families: 7B/13B/70B, seq 128/512/2048 to get real penalty numbers. Tag results with variance. (Priya to own.)
- Add a small UI prototype for subscription flow that shows the included SLA credit. (Diego to mock.)
- Draft 1-pager for sales with rules-of-thumb and three package examples. (Samira to draft.)

Random scratch thoughts:
- For developers, framing as "responsive tier" vs "best-effort tier" might be more intuitive than SLA-subsidy. "Responsive tier" includes a small monthly fee that covers priority and warm-cache.
- Consider using token buckets for fair usage with reserved slabs: tenant gets X tokens at reduced price, then pay-as-you-go above that.
- Avoid making subsidy conditional on complex metrics (p95 miss %, CPU utilization). Keep it simple: credit amount tied to reserved slab or committed spend.

End of sheet — aim to turn this into a tiny tool and a sales one-pager. Keep the calculator tiny and conservative; it's better to under-promise on subsidy than overcommit.
